name: Coaching and Evaluation
title: Coaching and Evaluation
answer: AI can help instructional coaches and principals turn their observation notes into clearer coaching conversations, but it should not be used to rate teachers through classroom video analysis. The distinction matters because coaching is meant to support growth, while evaluation affects a teacher's job, and the text says tools that give inconsistent ratings should stay out of that decision.

sections.body: This idea is about where AI belongs in the work of observing teachers and giving them feedback. Coaches and principals already watch teachers and talk with them about what they saw, and AI can help organize those notes into a useful summary of strengths and next steps. The coach still revises that summary before meeting the teacher, because the conversation itself is where growth happens. The problem it solves is the gap between raw observation notes and a focused coaching conversation, while drawing a firm line against using AI to judge teachers through video analysis.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a coach might use an approved tool to draft a summary from their own observation notes, then edit it before sitting down with the teacher. A principal might also use AI to summarize patterns across many brief classroom visits, for example how often students discuss ideas with each other, and use those trends to plan school wide professional learning rather than to judge individual teachers. The text does not give grade band examples, so the practice applies across the school rather than to a particular age group. Teachers should be told how walkthrough data is used, so the trends are not mistaken for evaluation.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with a study of eight AI models rating classroom videos. That study found their agreement with certified human observers was moderate at best, and their ratings changed from one run to the next (Melo et al., 2026). The models relied on what was said aloud and missed much of the context that trained observers see. The text uses this finding to argue that tools this inconsistent should not affect a teacher's job.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets a clear limit: AI analysis of classroom video should stay out of teacher evaluation. The reason given is that the models were only moderately in agreement with certified human observers, changed their ratings between runs, and missed context that trained observers notice. Walkthrough trends can still be useful, but only when kept separate from evaluation and used to guide professional learning without judging individual teachers. Teachers should know how walkthrough data is used, and the decisions about a teacher's job stay with people, not with the tool.
